c: Corroded or poorly seated connector between steering wheel harness and airbag module
Broken or worn conductor in the clock spring
Internal fault in the driver airbag module (stage 1 squib)
Chafed lead in the steering wheel or column harness
B0001.d: The restraint control module tests the firing loop of the first inflator stage in the driver airbag, which sits in the steering wheel hub and is fed through the clock spring. B0001 is stored when that loop is open, shorted or outside its resistance window; the fault byte added to the code names the exact type. Mercedes-Benz logs B000113 for an open stage 1 squib, Honda used B0001-13 on the 2013 Civic, Mitsubishi files it under the driver airbag module, FCA under squib 1, and GM on its 2020-21 full-size trucks, where B0001-1B came from rust particles at the airbag connector raising the resistance (bulletin 21-NA-005). Stage 1 is the charge used in every deployment, so a fault here can cost the driver frontal protection. The airbag warning lamp stays lit.
s: Airbag warning lamp or service airbag message stays on
Driver frontal airbag may not deploy in a crash
Safety note: do not probe the airbag circuit yourself; unplug airbag connectors only with the battery disconnected and the stated wait time observed

c: Open stage 2 squib lead at the airbag module connector
Stage 2 track in the clock spring broken
Replacement restraint module loaded with unsuitable software (Land Rover SSM 74577)
B0002.d: Dual-stage driver airbags hold a second charge that the restraint module fires only in severe crashes or after a short delay, so the cushion fills harder or for longer; a Nissan patent bases that choice on the change in vehicle speed and belt use. B0002 flags a fault in the firing loop of this second stage. Land Rover documents B0002-13 as an open stage 2 circuit on the Evoque, which also appeared after a module replacement had loaded older software (SSM 74577). Mercedes-Benz, Mitsubishi and FCA list it as the driver squib or module 2, GM as stage 2 of the steering wheel module. Because both stages share connector and clock spring, B0002 often comes together with B0001; alone it points to the stage 2 lead or squib. Adaptive inflation is lost and the airbag lamp is on.
s: Airbag warning lamp on
Driver airbag loses its second, high-severity stage
Safety note: do not probe the airbag circuit yourself; unplug airbag connectors only with the battery disconnected and the stated wait time observed

c: Connector position assurance lock at the airbag module not engaged
Third squib or vent valve squib in the airbag module faulty
Damaged clock spring conductor for the third circuit
B0003.d: Some driver airbag modules carry a third pyrotechnic element in addition to the two inflator stages, and B0003 covers its firing loop. FCA lists the code as driver frontal squib 3; its STAR case S2108000180 found B0003-2B (wires shorted together) next to B0001 and B0002 when connector locks behind the steering wheel were not engaged. Mercedes-Benz uses B000313 for the squib of the vent valve inside the driver airbag, which lets gas escape so the cushion becomes softer. An FCA patent describes such an active vent that the airbag electronics opens or keeps closed using data from occupant classification. With this loop faulted, the bag loses its third stage or adaptive venting, while the two inflator stages may still work. The airbag lamp lights up.
s: Airbag warning lamp on, often together with B0001 or B0002
Adaptive venting or third deployment stage unavailable
Safety note: do not probe the airbag circuit yourself; unplug airbag connectors only with the battery disconnected and the stated wait time observed

c: Faulty or loose knee airbag connector under the dash (Ford TSB 24-2444)
Harness pinched or damaged during work below the steering column
Internal fault in the knee airbag module
B0004.d: A knee airbag, also called an active knee bolster, sits in the lower dash below the steering column. It fills the space in front of the driver's knees and holds the lower body back in a frontal crash, mainly for unbelted occupants. B0004 reports a fault in its firing loop. Mercedes-Benz stores B000413 for an open squib of the driver kneebag. Ford lists B0004:1A with the passenger knee code B0013 on the 2024 Ranger and traces it to certain airbag connectors, recognisable by a number moulded into the connector lock (TSB 24-2444). In an IIHS study of more than 400 crash tests, knee airbags brought only a small benefit for belted dummies. Still, the restraint module counts the loop as part of the system, and the airbag lamp stays on until the circuit is repaired.
s: Airbag warning lamp on
Driver knee airbag may not deploy in a frontal crash
Safety note: do not probe the airbag circuit yourself; unplug airbag connectors only with the battery disconnected and the stated wait time observed

c: Restraint module configuration or software does not match the vehicle (Land Rover SSM 74577)
Open or shorted lead to the pyrotechnic column actuator
Faulty actuator in the steering column
B0005.d: Some steering columns can change how much energy they soak up while collapsing in a frontal crash. In a Delphi/Nexteer patent a controller fires pyrotechnic actuators that force an absorber strap into a tighter path or couple in extra absorbers, matching the column to driver size and crash severity. B0005 is the restraint module code for the firing loop of such an actuator. Land Rover documents B0005-56, an invalid or incompatible configuration, on the Evoque from 2018 when a replacement restraints control module had received older software than the factory level; a manual patch of the diagnostic equipment fixes it (SSM 74577). FMVSS 204 caps rearward column travel at 127 mm when the car hits a barrier at 48 km/h. With the loop faulted, the column keeps its fixed default behaviour and the airbag lamp is on.
s: Airbag warning lamp on
Adaptive energy absorption of the column unavailable, no effect on normal steering
Safety note: the column actuator is pyrotechnic; leave tests and connector work to a workshop with the battery disconnected

c: On Ram 1500 2025 the code belongs to the left stowage lid latch circuit of the body module, not the airbag
Driver airbag squib lead chafed against metal (ground short)
Insulation damage inside the clock spring
B0006.d: B0006 is missing from the public J2012 code lists, which go straight from B0005 to B0010. The only documented use found has nothing to do with airbags: on the 2025 Ram 1500 the body control module stores B0006-11 for a short to ground in the latch control of the left RamBox stowage lid, fixed by a module update (flash 08-204-24). The title describes a driver airbag firing loop shorted to ground. Current restraint modules report that as a fault byte on the stage code instead, for example GM B0012 02 on the 2011 Saab 9-4X, set after two seconds of ground short. A ground short in a squib circuit can stop the stage from firing, so the scan tool must first show which module stored B0006 before anyone works on the airbag.
s: Airbag warning lamp on when stored by the restraint module
On Ram 1500 2025 stowage lid will not open electrically, alarm may sound

c: On Ram 1500 2025 the code belongs to the right stowage lid latch circuit of the body module
Squib lead touching a powered wire in the column or steering wheel harness
Moisture bridging pins in a connector of the airbag circuit
B0007.d: Like B0006, this number is absent from the public J2012 lists. FCA uses B0007-11 on the 2025 Ram 1500 for the latch control of the right RamBox stowage lid, again a short to ground in the body control module and cured by the same flash 08-204-24; an airbag meaning is not documented anywhere. The title names a driver airbag loop shorted to battery voltage. Restraint modules treat that as a fault type of the stage code: GM sets B0012 01 or B0013 01 on the Saab 9-4X when the steering wheel airbag loop sits at supply voltage for two seconds. A short to positive is the more dangerous case because a further fault could energise the squib, so modules usually disable the affected stage and light the lamp. Confirm the storing module before any repair.
s: Airbag warning lamp on, affected stage disabled by the module
On Ram 1500 2025 right stowage lid inoperative

c: Loose, corroded or unlocked connector at the passenger airbag module
Harness damaged during dashboard or glovebox work
Internal fault in the passenger airbag module (stage 1 squib)
B0010.d: The front passenger airbag in the dashboard is normally dual-stage like the driver bag, but it also depends on occupant detection: FMVSS 208 allows it to be suppressed for small occupants and requires a readiness indicator that monitors the system. B0010 reports a fault in the firing loop of its first stage. Mercedes-Benz stores B001013 when the stage 1 squib of the passenger bag is open; Mitsubishi files B0010 under the passenger (assist) airbag module with several fault bytes. A suppressed airbag is not a fault and does not set this code; B0010 means the wiring or squib of stage 1 is electrically out of range. Typical spots are the connector behind the dash panel and harness routed past the glovebox. The passenger bag may not deploy and the airbag lamp stays lit.
s: Airbag warning lamp on
Front passenger airbag may not deploy in a crash
Safety note: do not probe the airbag circuit yourself; unplug airbag connectors only with the battery disconnected and the stated wait time observed

c: Poor contact on the stage 2 pins or open stage 2 lead
Stage 2 squib in the passenger airbag module faulty
Output stage in the restraint control module faulty
B0011.d: B0011 is the passenger counterpart of B0002: it concerns the second inflator stage of the dashboard airbag, which the module adds in severe crashes or fires with a delay. Mercedes-Benz logs B001113 for an open stage 2 squib of the front passenger airbag, and Mitsubishi lists B0011 as passenger airbag module 2. Stage 1 of the same bag has its own code B0010, a third element B0012. Since both stages leave the module through one connector, a code for stage 2 alone usually means a fault in the stage 2 pins, lead or squib rather than a general connector problem. Older GM modules (Saab 9-3 up to 2011) put passenger stage 2 faults under B0012 to B0014 instead. The airbag lamp is on and adaptive inflation for the passenger is lost.
s: Airbag warning lamp on
Passenger airbag loses its second stage for severe crashes

c: On GM vehicles weak terminal tension or chafed wires at the steering wheel airbag coil
Open or shorted third squib (vent valve) in the passenger airbag (J2012 meaning)
B0012.d: In the J2012 order B0012 is the third element of the front passenger airbag. Mercedes-Benz uses B001213 for the squib of the vent valve in that airbag, and Mitsubishi lists B0012 as passenger airbag module 3. GM gives the number a different meaning. Its later sensing and diagnostic modules assign B0012 to stage 1 of the steering wheel airbag; the Saab 9-4X 2011 manual trips it after two seconds of contact with supply or ground, an open, more than 4.4 ohms or less than 1.7 ohms; GM bulletins link it to chafed coil wires on the 2009 Cobalt and to weak terminal tension at the coil connector on the 2015 CTS. Older Saab 9-3 modules used B0012 for low resistance in the passenger stage 2 loop. Read the code with the maker's tool before choosing which airbag to check.
s: Airbag warning lamp on
Depending on maker, passenger airbag venting or GM driver airbag stage 1 affected

c: Faulty connector at the passenger knee airbag (Ford TSB 24-2444)
On GM vehicles fault in the driver airbag stage 2 loop or clock spring
Internal fault in the passenger knee airbag
B0013.d: B0013 belongs to the knee airbag on the passenger side, which deploys from the lower glovebox area and keeps the passenger's knees and thighs from sliding under the dash. Mercedes-Benz logs B001313 for an open squib of the front passenger kneebag. Ford pairs B0013:1A with the driver knee code B0004 on the 2024 Ranger; the TSB has all four airbag connectors checked, the passenger knee airbag being C2433, and swaps those with the wrong moulding number. GM uses the same number differently: in its later modules B0013 is stage 2 of the driver steering wheel airbag, with the same fault bytes as B0012 (Saab 9-4X 2011, GM 2009 Cobalt coil coverage). So a GM vehicle needs a check at the steering wheel, other makers at the passenger knee airbag. The airbag lamp is on.
s: Airbag warning lamp on
Passenger knee airbag (or on GM driver airbag stage 2) may not deploy

c: On GM vehicles loose or high-resistance side airbag connector under or in the driver seat
Seat harness chafed by seat frame, motor or foam
Internal fault in the airbag module served by this loop
B0014.d: B0014 is not in the public J2012 code lists; there the driver knee airbag has B0004 and the passenger knee airbag B0013. The number is documented only at General Motors, and with another meaning. GM modules from about 2010 use B0014 for the side airbag in the driver seat; the Saab 9-4X 2011 manual adds a fault byte for each failure, from a shorted or open loop to a high reading (0D, over 4.2 ohms) or a low one (0E, under 1.4 ohms). GM bulletins blame chafed or loose seat harness connectors and high connector resistance on Silverado and Tahoe 2014-15, Equinox, Traverse and the Bolt EV. Older Saab 9-3 modules used B0014 for a short in the passenger frontal stage 2 loop. A knee airbag meaning for this code is not publicly documented.

Affected airbag may not deploy

c: On GM vehicles loose or corroded connector at the driver belt pretensioner
Harness under the power seat rubbing on frame or seat motor (GM PIT4898C)
Internal fault in the pretensioner or airbag served by this loop
B0015.d: B0015 does not appear in the public J2012 code lists, which assign the passenger knee airbag to B0013. Only General Motors documents the number, as the firing loop of the belt pretensioner built into the driver's retractor. In the Saab 9-4X 2011 manual this pretensioner shares one diagnostic page with B001A, the anchor pretensioner, and both trip when their loop stays outside the allowed resistance band or touches supply or ground for two seconds. On the 2009-11 Impala GM notes that B0015 points to the retractor pretensioner while a second pretensioner sits at the belt anchor (PIC5396A). On an Equinox, a wire under the power seat rubbing on the seat motor set B0014 and B0015 and blew the seat fuse (PIT4898C). A passenger knee airbag under this number is not publicly documented. The airbag lamp is on.
s: Airbag warning lamp on, sometimes intermittent
On GM, belt pretensioner may not fire; power seat may fail if the harness is shorted
Safety note: do not probe the airbag circuit yourself; unplug airbag connectors only with the battery disconnected and the stated wait time observed

c: Squib leads shorted together or to ground in the passenger frontal loop (older GM)
Connector position assurance lock not seated (GM 08-09-41-002H)
On later GM vehicles fault in the left roof rail airbag loop
B0016.d: The public J2012 code lists skip B0016. General Motors used it in two generations with different meanings. In older modules, documented for the Saab 9-5 2006 and the Saab 9-3 up to 2011, B0016 means low resistance in the passenger frontal stage 1 loop: the reading drops under about 1.5 ohms, tolerance 0.2, for two seconds. That is close to the title, since a short to ground or between the leads also pulls the measured resistance down. In later GM modules (Saab 9-4X 2011) B0016 is the left roof rail airbag loop, with its own bytes for short to ground (02) and low resistance below 1.4 ohms (0E). GM bulletin 08-09-41-002H lists B0016 among codes caused by unseated connector locks on many 2005-14 GM models. The airbag lamp is on in every case.
s: Airbag warning lamp on
Passenger frontal airbag stage 1 (older GM) or left head airbag (later GM) may not deploy
Safety note: do not probe the airbag circuit yourself; unplug airbag connectors only with the battery disconnected and the stated wait time observed

c: On GM 2020-22 models faulty SDM software, cured by reprogramming (21-NA-176)
Open passenger frontal stage 1 loop (older GM meaning)
Squib lead in contact with a powered wire
B0017.d: None of the public J2012 lists contains B0017 either. In older GM modules (Saab 9-5 2006, Saab 9-3 up to 2011) it marks an open passenger frontal stage 1 loop, set once the loop reads more than roughly 4.5 ohms for two seconds, so the component matches the title but the fault type does not. Later GM vehicles use B0017 with GM's usual fault bytes, where 01 stands for short to battery. On the 2020-22 Acadia, XT4 and related models GM traced B0017 01, together with B0024 01 and B001E 01, to faulty SDM software rather than wiring: the code is cleared and the module reprogrammed (PIT5827, 21-NA-176). The parts named there are the knee airbag and the driver seat inboard side airbag. The airbag lamp is lit.

Affected airbag stage may be disabled

c: Open or shorted stage 1 loop of a first-row center frontal airbag (J2012 meaning)
On older GM/Saab passenger frontal stage 1 loop shorted to battery or ground
B0018.d: In the J2012 order of seating positions (driver, passenger, center, then second and third row) B0018 covers stage 1 of a frontal airbag for the middle seat of the first row. FMVSS 208 demands frontal airbags only for the outboard front seats, so such a bag is rare, and no carmaker publicly documents B0018 with this meaning. It is not the GM front center airbag of 2013, which deploys from the inner flank of the driver seat in side impacts (SAE 2013-01-1156). GM did use B0018 itself in older modules: on the Saab 9-5 2006 it reports a voltage out of range in the passenger frontal stage 1 circuit, above 4.1 V or below 1.0 V at module pin 44 for two seconds, and on the Saab 9-3 a short to battery or ground in that loop. Check which module stored the code.
s: Airbag warning lamp on
Affected frontal airbag stage may not deploy

c: On GM vehicles fretting corrosion in the passenger airbag in-line connector (HHR PI0117B)
Fault in the stage 2 loop of a first-row center frontal airbag (J2012 meaning)
Internal fault in the airbag module on this loop
B0019.d: B0019 is the stage 2 member of the first-row center frontal series B0018 to B001A, meant for the second inflator charge of a middle-seat frontal airbag. No carmaker publicly documents the code with this meaning. General Motors uses B0019 widely, but for stage 1 of the passenger airbag in the instrument panel: on the Saab 9-4X 2011 sub-codes 01 and 02 mark shorts, 04 an open, 0D a loop reading that stays high and 0E one that stays low, while stage 2 of that bag is B0020. On the 2009-10 Chevrolet HHR, fretting corrosion in the in-line connector between body and dash harness raised loop resistance and set B0019 0D or 04 (PI0117B and a customer satisfaction program). On GM vehicles the passenger airbag therefore needs checking first. The airbag lamp is on.
s: Airbag warning lamp on
On GM the passenger frontal airbag stage 1 may not deploy
Safety note: do not probe the airbag circuit yourself; unplug airbag connectors only with the battery disconnected and the stated wait time observed

c: On GM vehicles pinched, misrouted or corroded anchor pretensioner harness
Fault in the third stage loop of a first-row center frontal airbag (J2012 meaning)
B001A.d: B001A closes the first-row center frontal series and stands for a third stage of a middle-seat frontal airbag, matching B0003 for the driver and B0012 for the passenger. No carmaker documents it publicly in this sense. At General Motors the number belongs to the anchor-mounted belt pretensioner on the driver side, a second pretensioner at the belt end fitting that works next to the retractor unit coded B0015. Its limits match the other GM squib loops: a pretensioner loop reading beyond 4.2 ohms or beneath 1.4 ohms for two seconds sets the code, as do shorts and opens. GM bulletins report it on the 2009-11 Impala with a pinched or misrouted pretensioner harness (PIC5396A, 15-NA-074) and on Equinox and Traverse 2018 (PIE0438). On GM vehicles look at the lower belt anchor first. The airbag lamp is on.
s: Airbag warning lamp on
On GM the driver anchor pretensioner may not fire
Safety note: do not probe the airbag circuit yourself; unplug airbag connectors only with the battery disconnected and the stated wait time observed

c: Poor contact or corrosion at the side airbag connector or jumper harness under or in the seat
Internal fault in the left seat side airbag module
Pinched or chafed side airbag lead in the seat frame
Restraint module software reacting to interference, e.g. Toyota Tundra 2022 with wireless charger
B0020.d: B0020 covers the firing loop of the left front side airbag, the thorax bag usually built into the outer flank of the driver seat backrest. Toyota names B002011 and B002012 as short to ground and short to battery on the 2022 Tundra, where the wireless phone charger caused false entries that new SRS software cures (TSB005722). FCA reads B0020-13 as an open left seat squib on the 2014-17 Cherokee and the 2015-17 Chrysler 200 and fits new jumper harnesses in the seats (10-001-20). Honda collected parts from Accord, CR-V and TLX with the same byte 13, and Mitsubishi confirms each fault after 2 seconds. GM modules of about 2007-14 used B0020 for passenger frontal stage 2 instead, so check which bag the scan tool names. The airbag lamp is on.
s: Airbag warning lamp on
Left front side airbag may not deploy in a side impact

Damaged lead along the A-, B- or C-pillar or the roof rail
Internal fault in the left curtain airbag module
Fault or unsuitable software in the restraint control module
B0021.d: In the J2012 order B0021 is the first firing loop of the left curtain airbag, the bag that drops from the roof rail over the side windows. Mitsubishi files it under the left curtain module and stores byte 11, 12, 13 or a short to another circuit once the condition has lasted 2 seconds. Mercedes-Benz reads B002113 as an open squib of the left window bag on the A-Class, CLA and GLB, where raised contact resistance at the restraint unit plug was the cause (LI54.21-P-070658). Curtain 1 is the only or front curtain inflator; B0022 is the second one. GM Global A modules use B0021 for the passenger seat side airbag instead, with bulletins on seat harness contact (PI1469, 23-NA-030). Airbag lamp on; the left curtain may not fire.

Left curtain airbag may not deploy in a side impact or rollover

Damaged lead to the rear curtain section at the C-pillar or roof rail
Internal fault in the rear left curtain airbag module

B0022.d: B0022 belongs to a second firing loop for the left curtain airbag. Mercedes-Benz shows what that means in practice: on the A-Class, CLA and GLB, B002213 is an open squib in the left rear window bag, the curtain section for the rear seats, while B0021 serves the front one (LI54.21-P-070658, version 1 of 2019 and version 4 of 2020). Cars with a single curtain inflator never set it. General Motors has older meanings for the number: the 2006 Saab 9-5 used it for driver frontal stage 1 resistance below 2.0 ohms, and Global A modules for the passenger belt retractor pretensioner, as on the 2009-11 Impala (PIC5396A) or the Saab 9-4X. The module and descriptor shown by the scan tool decide which part is meant. Airbag lamp on.

B0023.d: B0023 does not appear in the J2012 code lists, which jump from B0022 to B0028, and no carmaker documents it as a ground short of a left side airbag stage. It is documented at General Motors with another meaning: in the Saab 9-4X 2011 manual B0023 is the right roof rail (curtain) airbag loop, with bytes for short to battery (01), short to ground (02), open (04) and resistance above 4.2 or below 1.4 ohms (0D, 0E), each confirmed after 2 seconds. GM bulletin 08-09-41-002H lists B0023 among codes caused by unseated connector position locks on many 2005-14 models. A real ground short in a squib loop can stop deployment, so first read which module and descriptor the scan tool reports. Airbag lamp on.

Worn clock spring in the driver airbag loop (older GM/Saab)
B0024.d: B0024 is missing from the public J2012 lists; there the right front side airbag is B0028. General Motors used the number twice. Older modules, such as those of the 2006 Saab 9-5 and the Saab 9-3, assign it to driver frontal stage 1: on the 9-5 the voltage at the module pin leaves the 1.0 to 4.1 volt window for 2 seconds, on the 9-3 the loop is shorted to ground or battery. In 2021 GM listed B0024 01 beside B0017 01 and B001E 01 on Cadillac XT4 to XT6, Blazer, Camaro, Malibu and Acadia as a software fault of the sensing module, pointing to the knee bag and the inboard side bag of the driver seat; new SDM software fixes it (PIT5827, 21-NA-176). A right side airbag meaning is not publicly documented. Airbag lamp on.

B0025.d: No public J2012 code list contains B0025, and no manufacturer publicly describes a second stage of a left side airbag under this number. The only trace is at General Motors: the Saab 9-4X 2011 manual groups B0025 with the roof rail airbag codes B0016 and B0023 but gives no descriptor for it. Two-stage side airbags are rare in any case. A Ford patent notes that thorax, pelvis and head bags usually have a single inflation setting because of their small size, and the dual-chamber side airbag described by Autoliv divides one cushion into chest and pelvis zones rather than firing twice. If B0025 appears, the descriptor and module name on the scan tool decide what is meant. Airbag lamp on; the affected bag may not deploy.

Open squib inside the airbag module
B0026.d: B0026 is missing from the public J2012 lists. General Motors documents it in older restraint modules with a meaning other than the title: on the 2006 Saab 9-5, B0026 is an open circuit in driver frontal stage 1, set when the measured resistance stays above 4.5 ohms, tolerance 0.2, for 2 seconds; the Saab 9-3 manuals add bytes for an open loop and too high resistance in the same driver circuit. Honda asked for parts from 2018-20 Accord and CR-V and from the 2015 TLX that stored B0028-13, an open or raised resistance in the passenger side airbag inflator. Mitsubishi confirms a short to ground after 2 seconds. The older GM numbering differs: the 2006 Saab 9-5 and the 9-3 used B0028 for low resistance in the passenger side bag loop, under 1.5 ohms. B0029.d: B0029 stands for the first firing loop of the right curtain airbag. In Ford's patent for rear belt monitoring the third-row bench is the hard-wired part of the system, while only the removable second row needs a wireless link. FMVSS 208 S7.5(c) extends the rear belt warning to all rear rows for vehicles built from September 2028. A Hall switch that senses the latched tongue is the usual hardware. No carmaker documents B0056 with this wording publicly, nor does any service bulletin mention it; Mitsubishi's B0052 is the documented model for this fault type.

B0057.d: In J2012, B0057 is the buckle sensor for the third row's centre seat, a position found only in eight-seat vans and SUVs. FMVSS 208 S7.5(c) will require a belt warning there from September 2028. No carmaker documents B0057 publicly with this meaning. Older GM airbag modules give the number a different job: the 2006 Saab 9-5 and the Saab 9-3 store B0057 when the passenger pretensioner loop resistance stays under 1.5 ± 0.2 ohms for 2 seconds. GM bulletin 14609 lists B0057 with B0058, B0059 and B0064 to B0066 on 2004-09 Colorado and Canyon extended cabs, whose rear door harness can suffer fatigue breaks and can disable the front pretensioners; GM extended coverage to 10 years. On older GM vehicles, check the pretensioner loop first.

B0058.d: B0058 is the J2012 code for the buckle sensor at the right seat of the third row. The sensor reports a latched or free belt to the module that runs the rear belt display, which FMVSS 208 S7.5(c) makes mandatory for every rear seat from September 2028. Fold-flat third rows and access from the right-hand sliding door put the lead under strain. No carmaker documents B0058 publicly with this meaning. Older GM modules again differ: on the 2006 Saab 9-5 B0058 means an open passenger pretensioner loop, with more than 4.5 ± 0.2 ohms for 2 seconds, while the Saab 9-3 also knows a high-resistance variant. GM bulletin 14609 for 2004-09 Colorado and Canyon extended cabs covers B0058 among the pretensioner codes caused by broken rear door wires.

c: Loose or corroded connector at the anchor-mounted tension sensor
Tension sensor output stuck or out of range, e.g. jammed slider
Sensor lead pinched under the seat or at the sill trim
B0060.d: B0060 refers to a belt tension sensor in the driver's belt, a force gauge usually bolted to the lower anchor with the webbing running through it. In Delphi's design a spring-loaded slider moves against the belt pull and a Hall element between two magnets turns the travel into a voltage; the springs give way at roughly 5 to 15 lb. CTS, which calls itself the market leader, builds such sensors in several mounting styles. A second Delphi patent has the sensor report its value in 3-lb steps over a two-wire line and flag readings outside the valid band as a high or low fault. Tension sensing serves mainly the passenger seat; a driver-side unit is rare. No carmaker documents B0060 publicly; Saab's older airbag modules do not list it. Airbag lamp on.
s: Airbag warning lamp on
Restraint module may fall back to a default firing strategy for the driver
Safety note: the sensor plug sits beside the seat near pretensioner and side airbag plugs; only unplug it with the battery disconnected and the wait time observed

c: Loose or corroded plug at the passenger belt tension sensor
Tension sensor reading out of range or stuck
Input fault in the occupant classification or airbag module
B0061.d: B0061 covers the belt tension sensor of the front passenger seat, a key input for passenger occupant classification. FMVSS 208 lets carmakers meet the child-seat rules for advanced airbags by fitting a system that automatically switches the passenger airbag off for small occupants. A child seat strapped in tightly presses into the cushion and can look as heavy as an adult on the weight sensor; the tension sensor exposes that. Delphi's patent lets the occupant module subtract belt load from seat weight and suppress the airbag above a calibrated pull of about 30 lb, and the sensor reports out-of-range values as faults. No carmaker documents B0061 publicly with this meaning. Saab 9-3 modules use it for a low driver curtain loop resistance.

c: Knee airbag lead chafed against a dash bracket or steering column part
Damaged knee airbag connector after work under the dashboard

B0062.d: None of the publicly available J2012 code lists contain B0062; they jump from B0061 to B0070, and no carmaker describes it with the knee airbag meaning shown in the title. J2012 files knee airbag loops under B0004 for the driver and B0013 for the passenger, with the fault type in the added byte; Mercedes-Benz logs kneebag squib faults as B000413 and B001313, and in that scheme a grounded loop would carry byte 11 instead. The only public use of B0062 is at Saab: 9-3 airbag modules (manuals of 2003 and 2007) store it for the driver-side curtain or rollover bar loop, with byte 04 for open and 0E for resistance too high. Knee airbags sit in the lower dash; an IIHS study of 414 crash tests found little overall benefit for belted drivers.
s: Airbag warning lamp on

c: Pretensioner leads shorted together, e.g. squashed harness at the B-pillar
Colorado/Canyon extended cab: fatigued wires in the rear door harness (bulletin 14609)

B0064.d: No publicly available J2012 code list includes B0064; there, B0060 names the driver belt tension sensor. Older airbag modules from General Motors do use it: on the 2006 Saab 9-5, B0064 is set when the resistance of the driver pretensioner loop stays below 1.5 ohms, with a 0.2-ohm tolerance, for 2 seconds; B0065 marks an interrupted loop and B0066 a voltage at pin 34 outside 1.0 to 4.1 V. Saab 9-3 manuals of 2003 and 2007 describe the same fault as too little resistance at the driver's belt tensioner. The module still attempts to fire the pretensioner in a crash. GM bulletin 14609 names B0064 among the codes caused by fatigue breaks in the rear door harness of Colorado and Canyon extended cab trucks, model years 2004 to 2009. Airbag lamp on.
s: Airbag warning lamp on

Firing lead chafed by seat rails or trim clips
Interference from added electronics, e.g. a wireless charger (Toyota Tundra 2022, ECU update)
Internal fault in the pretensioner squib
B0070.d: B0070 covers the firing loop of the driver's first (A) belt pretensioner, the squib the airbag module ignites to take slack out of the belt in a crash. A short or open in that loop lets the module no longer count on the device, so it lights the airbag lamp. Toyota names the code in exactly this sense: its Tundra bulletin T-SB-0057-22 (model year 2022) lists B007011 (short to ground) and B007012 (short to battery), there triggered by the wireless Qi charger and cured by reprogramming the SRS ECU. J2012 does not fix which device is A; GM notes that a front seat may carry a retractor, buckle or anchor pretensioner, or more than one. Mitsubishi logs its front retractor units under its own codes B1029/B102A. Saab 9-3 airbag modules use B0070 for the passenger curtain loop instead.
s: Airbag warning lamp on
Driver belt is not tightened in a crash; airbags themselves are usually unaffected
Safety note: the pretensioner is a pyrotechnic part; work on it only with the battery disconnected and the wait time observed, ideally at a specialist workshop

c: Plug under the front bench centre seat loose or corroded

Airbag module configured for a centre pretensioner the vehicle does not have
Internal fault of the centre pretensioner
B0071.d: B0071 is reserved for a pretensioner at the middle seat of the first row, which exists only where a three-person front bench is fitted. The airbag module would watch this squib like any other firing loop and flag an open, a short or a resistance outside its window. No carmaker publishes B0071 with this meaning. Mercedes-Benz does show that such a device can be present: its information LI54.21-P-070658 (A-, CLA-, GLB-Class) lists an open circuit at the emergency tensioning retractor in the centre of the first seat row, but files it under its own code B1B36. GM places buckle pretensioners at the inner flank of a front seat. In the airbag modules of the Saab 9-3 (2003, 2007), B0071 stands for a short in the passenger curtain or rollover-bar circuit, a different part altogether.

Middle front occupant gets no belt pretensioning in a crash

c: Passenger pretensioner plug not latched or corroded
Lead pinched at the passenger seat base or B-pillar trim
Interference from added electronics such as a wireless charger
B0072.d: B0072 reports a fault in the deployment loop of the front passenger's A-stage belt pretensioner. While that loop is faulty the device cannot be relied on to fire, so the airbag module lights its lamp and keeps the code. Toyota uses the number this way: T-SB-0057-22 for the 2022 Tundra and Tundra Hybrid lists B007212, a short to battery, among the codes the wireless charger can provoke, and the remedy is an SRS ECU reprogramming. The passenger seat often carries further devices; Mercedes logs the passenger's belt end fitting tensioner and retractor as B007A and B007F, and FCA ties B007F to the passenger retractor at the B-pillar. NHTSA's 2013 evaluation explains how buckle and retractor pretensioners remove slack. Whatever the hardware, a stored B0072 means passenger pretensioning is not assured.
s: Airbag warning lamp on
Front passenger belt may stay slack in a crash
Safety note: the pretensioner is pyrotechnic; only handle it de-energised (battery off, wait time) and have it serviced at a specialist workshop

B0073.d: B0073 concerns the pretensioner at the left outer seat of the second row, normally built into the rear retractor. Mitsubishi documents it under exactly this name: with the ignition on, its airbag sensor unit stores B0073 with byte 11, 12, 13, 1A or 1B for a short to ground, a short to power, an open, lines shorted to each other or excessive resistance, and with byte 55 when the stored configuration does not match the vehicle; each fault must last 2 seconds. Toyota's Tundra bulletin T-SB-0057-22 lists B007311 and B007312. IIHS frontal tests with a dummy in the left rear seat show why such units are now spreading to the back row. GM uses the number differently: bulletin 22-NA-170 for the Equinox and Terrain links B0073 to water in the right front seat harness connector X320.

Left rear occupant gets no belt pretensioning in a crash

c: On GM vehicles, fault in the passenger presence sensor mat or its pinched wire (older GM meaning)

Open or short in the harness to the rear centre seat
B0074.d: B0074 would flag the firing loop of a pretensioner at the second row's middle seat. Rear centre belts with their own pretensioner are rare; IIHS rear-seat tests concentrate on the outboard positions, and no carmaker publishes B0074 with the J2012 meaning. The code is common in GM vehicles, but with an older meaning: the 2011 Saab 9-4X sets B0074 00/04 when the passenger presence module loses its seat sensor mat, GM's Impala bulletin PIE0485A (2015–2018) covers B0074-0D, and campaign N182188910 for the 2017 Buick Verano ties B0074 0D/0E to a pinched presence sensor wire that suppresses the passenger airbag. In a GM vehicle, B0074 therefore points to the front passenger seat sensing, not a rear belt. Where the code does mean a rear centre pretensioner, the airbag lamp is on and that unit is inactive.

Interference from added electronics, fixed by an ECU update (Toyota Tundra 2022)
Internal fault of the right rear pretensioner
B0075.d: B0075 is the right-hand counterpart of B0073: the pretensioner at the second row's right outer seat. Mitsubishi lists it as PRE-TEN REAR RH with the J2012 title and tests the circuit whenever the ignition is on; byte 11 stands for a short to ground and 13 for an open circuit, while further bytes cover shorts to power, crossed wires, high resistance or a configuration mismatch, each after 2 seconds. Toyota names B007512, a short to battery, in its 2022 Tundra bulletin about the Qi charger. Rear retractor wiring passes through seat and trim areas that are opened during interior work, which makes a disturbed plug the usual suspect. With the code active, the airbag lamp is on and the right rear passenger may not be pulled back into the seat in a crash.

Right rear occupant without belt pretensioning in a crash

Airbag module coded for a third-row pretensioner that is not fitted
B0076.d: B0076 belongs to the pretensioner at the left seat of the third row, a position found only in vehicles with a third seat row. No carmaker publishes B0076 with this meaning. Mercedes shows how third-row units are logged in practice: its LI54.21-P-070658 names open-circuit faults of the emergency tensioning retractors at the left and right of the third seat row as B00E7 and B00E6, the C-stage slots, so a B0076 is not to be expected on those models. The circuit itself is a pyrotechnic squib that the airbag module checks for opens, shorts and resistance drift, as with the front retractor and buckle units GM and NHTSA describe. If B0076 is stored, the airbag lamp is on and the third-row left occupant may not get any pretensioning.

Airbag module coded for a centre pretensioner that is not installed
B0077.d: B0077 stands for the pretensioner at the middle seat of the third row. Hardly any vehicle fits one, and no manufacturer documents B0077 with this J2012 meaning; Mercedes, which equips some models with third-row tensioning retractors, lists only a left and a right unit (B00E7/B00E6). The number is met more often in older GM-built Saabs. The 2006 Saab 9-5 stores B0077 when the airbag module cannot communicate with the driver-side side-impact sensor because of an open or a short, and Saab 9-3 modules of 2003 and 2007 use it for the driver-side B-pillar sensor. On such cars the fault lies in the door or pillar sensor, not in a rear belt. For a genuine third-row centre pretensioner, a stored code means a lit airbag lamp and a disabled unit.

Plug at the third-row right belt loosened when the seat was folded or removed
Internal fault of the third-row right pretensioner
B0078.d: B0078 refers to the right seat of the third row and its belt pretensioner. No carmaker publishes B0078 in this J2012 sense, and Mercedes models with third-row tensioning retractors log the right-hand unit as B00E6 instead. Like B0077, the number has a sensor meaning in GM's older Saab modules: the 2006 Saab 9-5 sets B0078 for an open or short in the communication with the passenger-side side-impact sensor, and the 9-3 airbag module (2003, 2007) uses it for the passenger-side B-pillar sensor, with bytes for faulty communication, a short to battery or ground, or a wrong sensor fitted. Where the code really concerns the right pretensioner of the third row, the airbag lamp is on and that seat loses its pretensioning until the loop is repaired.

Internal fault of the end fitting tensioner squib
B0079.d: B0079 marks the driver's second (B) pretensioner. Mercedes-Benz uses the code in exactly this way: in LI54.21-P-070658, valid for A-Class, CLA and GLB, B007913 is an open circuit in the squib of the belt end fitting tensioner on the driver's side, while the retractor of the same seat appears as B007E. An end fitting or anchor pretensioner pulls on the lower belt anchor next to the door side of the seat and so tightens the lap section; GM's restraint guide and a Hyundai-Kia patent describe this layout. Older Saab models give the number another meaning: the 2006 Saab 9-5 stores B0079 when an incorrect driver-side side-impact sensor is installed. A stored B0079 lights the airbag lamp and means the driver's lap tensioner may not fire.

Lead to the lap tensioner pinched under the passenger seat
Internal fault of the passenger lap tensioner
B007A.d: B007A is the passenger-side twin of B0079 and covers the second pretensioner on the front passenger seat. Mercedes lists B007A13 for an open in the squib of the passenger's belt end fitting tensioner on the A-, CLA- and GLB-Class and keeps the passenger retractor apart as B007F. A lap or anchor pretensioner of this kind fires together with the retractor unit, as Joyson explains for its lap pretensioner, and draws the lap belt down onto the pelvis to cut the risk of sliding under it. Mitsubishi files comparable lap pretensioners under its own codes B1001 and B1002 rather than in J2012 slots, so B007A is not expected there. Once B007A is set, the airbag lamp comes on and the module records that the passenger's lap tensioning is unavailable.

B007B.d: B007B would cover a second pretensioner on the outboard left seat in row two, for example a lap tensioner in addition to the retractor unit. No manufacturer publishes B007B. The documented rear cases use other slots: Mitsubishi files its left rear retractor pretensioner under B0073, and Mercedes logs the left rear emergency tensioning retractor as B00E3, the C-stage code. Joyson's lap pretensioner shows the kind of hardware a B stage could stand for, since it is meant to fire alongside a retractor pretensioner. In IIHS crash tests that placed a dummy behind the driver, submarining showed up in some vehicles with rear pretensioners, which is the risk such a lap device addresses. A stored B007B keeps the airbag lamp lit and leaves that stage inactive.
s: Airbag warning lamp on
Left rear lap belt not tightened in a crash

Airbag module configuration lists a stage that is not installed
Internal fault of the right rear B-stage tensioner
B007C.d: B007C is the second-row right counterpart of B007B: an additional pretensioner stage at the right outer rear seat. No manufacturer publishes this code. On that seat Mitsubishi uses B0075 for its retractor pretensioner and Mercedes uses B00E4 for the right rear emergency tensioning retractor, so neither leaves a role for B007C. A B stage would typically be a buckle or anchor unit acting on the lap belt; NHTSA's 2013 evaluation explains how a buckle pretensioner pulls the buckle down by a cable and piston, while Joyson describes lap tensioners working with the retractor. Rear lap units are far less common than front ones, so this code is unusual. When it does appear, the airbag lamp stays on and that stage cannot be counted on.
s: Airbag warning lamp on
Right rear lap belt not pretensioned in a crash

Harness under the rear bench chafed or pinched
B007D.d: B007D names a second pretensioner at the middle seat of the second row. No carmaker documents it, and since even one pretensioner at the rear centre seat is uncommon, a second stage there is rarer still. Where such hardware is fitted, the B stage would act on the buckle or anchor side, comparable to the Autoliv pulley-and-cable buckle tensioner of patent US7360795B2 or the buckle units GM shows at the inner flank of front seats. Wiring to a rear centre position runs through the seat base or floor and can be disturbed when a split bench is folded or taken out. The firing loop is monitored like every other squib circuit. A stored B007D lights the airbag lamp, and the module treats that stage as unavailable.
s: Airbag warning lamp on
Rear centre occupant without the second pretensioning stage

B007E.d: B007E is the driver's third (C) pretensioner circuit. Mercedes-Benz fills this slot with the retractor: in LI54.21-P-070658 for the A-, CLA- and GLB-Class, B007E13 is an open circuit at the squib of the driver's emergency tensioning retractor, with B0079 for the belt end fitting tensioner and B0080 for the driver's belt force limiter. The retractor unit is housed either inside the B-pillar or within the seat and winds the spool back to remove slack from the shoulder belt, as GM and Joyson explain. The same Mercedes list puts the rear retractors on the C codes B00E3, B00E4, B00E6 and B00E7, so there the C stage consistently means the retractor. A stored B007E means the airbag lamp is on and the driver's shoulder belt will not be pretensioned.

Body harness pinched between B-pillar trim retainer and body (FCA S2008000137)
Internal fault of the passenger retractor pretensioner
B007F.d: B007F covers the passenger's third (C) pretensioner and is the best-documented code of this series. Mercedes lists B007F13 as an open in the squib of the front passenger's emergency tensioning retractor (A-, CLA- and GLB-Class). FCA uses the same slot for the same part: STAR case S2008000193 for the 2020–2021 Ram 1500 links B007F-2B to a loose or spread plug of the retractor down at the passenger-side B-pillar, repaired with kit 68148100AA, and case S2008000137 for the 2020 Jeep Grand Cherokee reports B007F-11, a short to ground, from a body harness pinched by B-pillar trim. The retractor is a pyrotechnic unit that rewinds the webbing in a crash. With B007F set, the airbag lamp is on and the passenger's shoulder belt lacks pretensioning.

Passenger shoulder belt not tightened in a crash

c: Raised contact resistance at the airbag module connector (Mercedes LI54.21-P-070658)

Internal fault of the load limiter squib in the retractor
B0080.d: B0080 reports a fault in the firing loop that switches the driver's belt force limiter. In adaptive retractors a small squib, fired by the airbag module, changes the level at which the webbing is paid out, so the chest load suits crash severity and occupant. Mercedes-Benz uses the code exactly so: topic LI54.21-P-070658 (cars of the 177, 118 and 247 series) gives B008013 for an interrupted igniter of the driver's belt force limiter, traced to raised resistance at the airbag module plug. Ford names B0080 among the restraint module codes cured by reprogramming on 2017–2018 Fusion/MKZ, without giving its meaning. Older GM-built Saabs (9-3, 9-5) use B0080 for an internal fault of the driver-side B-pillar or side impact sensor instead. With the code set, the airbag lamp is lit.

c: On GM vehicles, fault or mismatch of the passenger presence module in the seat (different meaning)

Internal fault of the centre seat load limiter squib
B0081.d: B0081 is assigned to a squib-switched limiter for the centre place of a three-across front bench. No carmaker publishes the code with this meaning. Mercedes-Benz files a first-row centre tensioning retractor under its own code B1B36, and NHTSA's 2013 study notes that load limiters became universal only at the two outer front seats. In practice the number almost always carries a GM meaning: on Global A cars such as the Saab 9-4X it means a passenger presence module fault (00) or a wrong module fitted (3A), with the passenger airbag disabled; GM special coverage N182188910 (2017 Buick Verano) and bulletin PIE0407B (Impala) deal with it. Saab 9-3 and 9-5 airbag modules use B0081 for a wrong passenger-side B-pillar or side sensor. Check the make before suspecting a belt.

On GM vehicles the passenger airbag status shows OFF although an adult is seated

c: Poor connection at the passenger retractor plug (Ford C303B, SSM 51998)
Raised resistance at the airbag module connector (Mercedes LI54.21-P-070658)
Internal fault of the passenger retractor and limiter assembly
B0082.d: B0082 covers the firing loop of the front passenger's switchable belt force limiter. Two manufacturers document this meaning. In the Mercedes A-Class, CLA and GLB, B008213 marks an interrupted igniter of the passenger-side belt force limiter. Ford special service message 51998 covers 2023 Escape, Corsair, Bronco Sport and Maverick that store B0082:1A because of the passenger belt retractor at connector C303B; where a connection fault is found, the retractor and pretensioner assembly is replaced before any wiring repair. Autoliv patents show why retractor and limiter belong together: the pretensioner's own gas can select the higher limiting level. On GM Global A cars (Saab 9-4X) B0082 means the seat belt reminder sensor in the passenger cushion instead. The airbag lamp stays on.

FMVSS 226 requires a monitored readiness indicator where ejection mitigation deploys in a rollover; Karma recalled the 2018 Revero because its rollover sensing was not enabled. B009B.d: B009B names a fifth crash sensor on the left side. No carmaker documents this code publicly, and the reviewed bulletins and airbag indexes stop well before it. Why vehicles carry several side satellites at all follows from FMVSS 214: cars must protect occupants in a moving barrier crash and in a vehicle-to-pole test, and a narrow pole can strike anywhere along the side. Continental offers two kinds of satellites for this: the gSAT reports acceleration from rigid structure, the pSAT reacts to the pressure rise of a crushed door. A fifth left unit would most likely monitor a rear door or an extra seat row. When B009B is stored, the module has rejected that sensor's signal or circuit, and side or curtain airbags may react later on that side. The airbag lamp is lit.

Seat weight systems often measure at the corners: a CTS patent puts one thick-film strain gauge sensor at each corner between seat pan and slide rail, so the occupant's whole weight passes through four bridges whose leads meet in one junction box before the airbag controller. In such a layout every corner could carry its own letter, which would explain a series from A onward, yet no public source confirms that order. A stored B00B1 therefore means one load input is open, out of range or implausible; seat bolts fitted with the wrong torque and harness strain after seat removal are typical suspects. Honda's job aid for its passenger seat weight sensors shows the service side: the sensors sit in the seat base or frame, need recalibration after a sensor or unit is replaced, and a binding sensor may be freed by loosening, shaking and retorquing the seat. B00BA.d: B00BA covers position input D, the fourth of the driver seat sensors. Its use by a carmaker is not documented publicly. Early out-of-position concepts mixed several sensor kinds: a 1989 Automotive Systems Laboratory patent uses a pyroelectric detector for presence, ultrasound for the distance to wheel and dashboard and a pressure transducer under the occupant for weight, recommends redundant sensors of each kind against false readings, warns the occupant with a lamp and fires a multi-cartridge driver inflator step by step to match size and position. B00BB.d: B00BB is the fifth and last driver seat occupant position sensor in the J2012 block. No carmaker publishes this code. FMVSS 208 leaves both the suppression zone and the choice of sensors to the maker. Some classification signals are not a weight at all but a frequency, which makes them prone to electrical noise. Tesla reported for 2017–2019 Model 3 cars that the OCS frequency could leave its valid range because of interference on the passenger seat harness, so the airbag symbol appeared on the touchscreen. The first fix added a harness extension with a ferrite filter at the OCS module, which sits under the front of the seat; a later bulletin used a dedicated filter module, each about 0.15 h of labour. c: Open or shorted lead to the chime or speaker used for restraint warnings
Chime module or cluster speaker failed
Tone request from the restraint module not received by the sounding unit
B00D4.d: B00D4 concerns the audible restraint warning, the tone that stands in when a fault cannot be shown by the lamp. Ford's 2014 F-150 manual describes it: system readiness is signalled by the warning light, or by a backup tone if the light is out, and a problem announces itself as five beeps in a row, repeated until the fault and the lamp are put right. Audi's 1986 patent explains why such a fallback exists: a blown fuse could kill both the airbag module and its lamp, so the driver would believe the system was fine; it mentions an audible alarm as an alternative signal. No carmaker publishes B00D4. A stored code means the restraint module sees a fault in its chime or speaker path, so a later lamp failure could go wholly unannounced.
s: No warning tone where one would be expected, other warning chimes may also be silent
Airbag warning lamp on
Safety note: fallback warning missing; work on cluster and restraint wiring only de-energised (ignition off, battery off, wait time), specialist workshop

c: Indicator lead shorted to ground, shorted to power or open (Mitsubishi -11/-12/-13)
Passenger airbag off indicator itself failed
Network or gateway software fault, as on 2021 Ford Edge/Nautilus (SSM 50127)
Internal fault of the airbag control unit output
B00D5.d: B00D5 concerns the lamp that tells the front occupants the passenger airbag is off. FMVSS 208 wants it yellow, worded PASSENGER AIR BAG OFF (short form PASS AIR BAG OFF) and separate from the readiness lamp; Ford's 2014 F-150 places it by the radio and lights it briefly at start as a self-test. Mitsubishi defines the code in its 2022 airbag index as PASS A/B INDICATOR: subtype -11 for a short to ground, -12 for a short to power and -13 for an open circuit, each checked with the ignition on and set after 2 s; harness, the indicator itself or the airbag control unit are listed as causes. Ford logged B00D5:01 in the restraint module of 2021 Edge and Nautilus among network faults, cured by updating the gateway module. Occupants may be misled about the airbag.
s: Passenger airbag off lamp stays dark during the start check or shows the wrong state
Airbag warning lamp on
Safety note: occupants cannot see whether the passenger airbag is off; do not fit a rear-facing child seat until repaired, wiring only de-energised, specialist workshop

c: Switch circuits present in the harness of a vehicle without the switch, damaged or picking up faults (FCA B00DF-95)
Key switch worn or its lead open or shorted
Restraint module software counter or configuration error (Ford B00DF:4A)
B00DF.d: B00DF is set for the key switch that lets the passenger airbag be turned off by hand. FMVSS 208 S4.5.4 allowed it on vehicles built before September 2012 with no forward rear seats or a short rear row; it must take the key, stay apart from the ignition and keep the bag off until switched back, and 49 CFR 595.5 governs retrofits under an NHTSA letter. Two makers use the code. FCA describes B00DF-95, incorrect assembly, on 2018–2021 Jeep Wrangler built without the on/off switch option CGZ: unused dash harness circuits R167/R168 should be checked and isolated at the ORC. Ford reports B00DF:4A after self-tests on 2024 Nautilus, from an internal counter fixed over the air, and on 2026–2027 Transit, cleared with FDRS. A real fault lights the airbag lamp.
s: Airbag warning lamp on
Passenger airbag does not follow the switch position, or the off lamp disagrees with it

c: Plug of the lap or anchor tensioner at the left third-row seat loose, unlatched or corroded
Lead strained or chafed by folding and stowing the third-row seat
Airbag module coded for a B stage the vehicle does not have (after module or seat replacement)
Internal open or short in the tensioner squib
B00E0.d: B00E0 points to a second pretensioner stage (B) on the left seat of the third row. Such a stage would be an extra device next to the retractor, typically a lap or anchor tensioner that pulls on the lower belt end. No carmaker publishes B00E0. Mercedes-Benz, which does fit third-row tensioners (the 2017 GLS manual lists them for every third-row belt), logs the left third-row retractor under B00E7 in topic LI54.21-P-070658, i.e. on the C slot, and never names a B stage back there. GM describes anchor units only for front seats, and Joyson pairs its lap pretensioner with a retractor unit against submarining. A stored code lights the airbag lamp; the stage is treated as not available.
s: Airbag warning lamp lit
Lap belt at the left third-row seat may not be pulled tight in a crash
Safety note: pyrotechnic part – work only with the battery disconnected and the wait time observed, preferably at a specialist workshop

c: Connector of the right third-row buckle or anchor tensioner not fully seated
Wiring under the cargo floor or side trim pinched or damaged by loads
Raised contact resistance at the airbag module plug
B00E1.d: On the right seat of the third row, B00E1 stands for a B-stage tensioner whose firing loop shows an open, a short or an out-of-window resistance. In no public service document does a manufacturer use B00E1. Where Mercedes-Benz fits a right third-row tensioner, it is the retractor, and the airbag unit reports it as B00E6 (LI54.21-P-070658, versions of March and June 2020). A B stage there would be a buckle or anchor device; NHTSA's 2013 study of pretensioners explains how a buckle unit drags the buckle down by a cable when its charge fires, and GM lists buckle, retractor and anchor units as the three possible types. Expect a lit airbag lamp and no tensioning from this stage until the loop is repaired.
s: Airbag lamp on in the instrument cluster
Occupant at the right of the third row gets no B-stage tensioning
Safety note: the tensioner contains a pyrotechnic charge; only work on it de-energised (battery off, wait time) and leave it to a specialist workshop

c: Module variant coding expects a centre B stage that is not installed
Plug under the third-row centre seat disconnected after seat removal
Squib of the centre lap tensioner open or shorted internally
B00E2.d: B00E2 would report the firing circuit of a B-stage tensioner at the centre seat of the third row. This is about the rarest slot in the pretensioner table: a centre seat in row three is uncommon, and a second tensioner stage on it even more so. No manufacturer documents the code. For comparison, the third-row tensioners in Mercedes vehicles are listed only as left and right retractor loops (B00E7/B00E6 in LI54.21-P-070658), and the GLS manual of 2017 likewise speaks of retractor tensioners. A B stage would act on the lap section, as Joyson's lap pretensioner does in combination with a retractor. If the code appears, check first whether the module's equipment coding matches the seats actually fitted.
s: Airbag indicator stays on after the self-test
Centre occupant of the third row may lack lap-belt tensioning in a crash
Safety note: pyrotechnic restraint component – disconnect the battery, wait the specified time and have the work done by a specialist

c: Retractor pretensioner plug not latched after trim or seat work (Jeep Wrangler 2023, connector D3244A)
High contact resistance at the airbag control unit connector (Mercedes LI54.21-P-070658)
Lead to the left rear retractor chafed at the C-pillar or seat frame
Faulty squib in the retractor pretensioner
B00E3.d: B00E3 is the C-stage tensioner of the left outer rear seat, and two makers document it codegenau. Stellantis case S2408000089 (Jeep Wrangler 2023) has the occupant restraint controller store B00E3-13, named there for the retractor tensioner at the left of row two, after a service visit; the fix was to secure connector D3244A with a push-pull-push check, no parts. Mercedes-Benz topic LI54.21-P-070658 (A-Class, CLA, later GLB) reads B00E313 as an open squib in the tensioning retractor behind the left rear passenger, usually caused by high contact resistance at the airbag unit plug; reconnecting comes first, a new control unit only if the fault returns. So C here means the retractor, as Joyson's pyrotechnic retractor describes. Airbag lamp on.
s: Airbag warning lamp or SRS message in the cluster
Left rear shoulder belt is not retracted in a crash
Safety note: the retractor pretensioner is pyrotechnic; work only with the system de-energised (battery off, wait time) and preferably at a specialist workshop

c: Poor contact at the SRS control unit plug (Mercedes A-Class/CLA/GLB)
Plug at the right rear retractor loose after trim removal
Airbag control unit itself faulty (fault returns after reconnecting)
Squib in the right rear retractor open
B00E4.d: B00E4 belongs to the outboard seat on the right in the back and its C-stage tensioner. Mercedes-Benz uses it in that sense: every version of LI54.21-P-070658 seen here (December 2019 to June 2020) lists B00E413 as an open in the squib of the tensioning retractor at the rear right. The topic blames higher resistance at the SRS unit connector rather than the tensioner and tells technicians to trace the wire, reseat the plugs and replace the unit only on recurrence. The retractor sits behind the rear trim or in the seat and winds the webbing back when fired, as GM's rescue guide and Joyson explain. No public bulletin from another maker cites B00E4. While the code is stored, the airbag lamp or SRS message stays on.
s: SRS message or airbag lamp permanently displayed
Right rear passenger loses shoulder-belt tensioning
Safety note: pyrotechnic tensioner – only work on it with the battery disconnected and after the wait time, ideally at a specialist workshop

c: Centre-seat tensioner plug under the rear bench not engaged
Module coded for a centre tensioner that the vehicle lacks
Lead damaged where it passes the split or folding rear bench hinge
B00E5.d: B00E5 covers a C-stage tensioner at the middle seat of row two. No manufacturer publishes it. Rear centre tensioners are scarce: Mercedes' 2017 GLS manual names tensioners only for the outer second-row belts, and the Mercedes bulletin that assigns B00E3 and B00E4 to the outer rear retractors has no centre entry. IIHS research on rear occupants (2020) states that belt countermeasures for the rear are available yet rarely fitted, so such slots often stay empty. If a vehicle does carry a centre retractor or buckle tensioner, the airbag module watches its squib like any other and sets B00E5 for an open, a short or a resistance drift; the warning lamp then comes on and that seat loses its tensioning.
s: Airbag lamp on
Rear centre passenger may not be held back early in a frontal crash
Safety note: the tensioner holds a pyrotechnic charge – battery off, wait time observed, repair at a specialist workshop

c: Contact resistance at the airbag unit connector (Mercedes LI54.21-P-070658)
Plug of the right third-row retractor behind the cargo trim loose
Wiring in the rear wheel arch area pinched by trim or cargo
Squib of the right third-row retractor defective
B00E6.d: Note the order in this block: B00E6 is the right seat of the third row, while B00E7 is the left. Mercedes-Benz fills B00E6 with the retractor tensioner on that seat: LI54.21-P-070658 (first issued December 2019 for A-Class and CLA, extended to GLB in version 4) reads B00E613 as an interrupted igniter in the tensioning retractor on the right of row three. The stated cause is again contact resistance at the airbag unit plug. Mercedes' GLS manual of 2017 confirms that the brand gives third-row belts their own tensioners and force limiters. No other maker publishes the code. With B00E6 stored, the airbag lamp is on and the right third-row belt will not be tightened.
s: SRS message or airbag warning lamp
Right third-row belt stays slack in a crash
Safety note: work on this pyrotechnic retractor only de-energised (battery disconnected, wait time) and preferably by a specialist

c: Raised resistance at the restraint unit plug
Left third-row retractor connector disturbed during trim or seat work
Control unit below the required level, fault keeps returning
B00E7.d: B00E7 marks the C-stage tensioner of the third row's left seat, listed after its right-hand twin B00E6. Mercedes-Benz documents it: LI54.21-P-070658 uses B00E713 when the firing pill of the left third-row tensioning retractor shows an open, in the same list as the rear and driver retractors. In that topic the remedy does not start with the tensioner but with fault-tracing the wire and reconnecting the restraint unit plugs; only a recurring fault calls for a new control unit of at least level Q4. Joyson describes this kind of pyrotechnic retractor, which can sit in the body or the seat structure. No other maker publishes B00E7. Airbag lamp on; the left third-row occupant is not tensioned.
s: Airbag lamp or fixed SRS message
No pretensioning for the left third-row seat
Safety note: pyrotechnic device – disconnect the battery and wait before touching it; have it serviced at a specialist workshop

c: Connector of the seat-mounted centre retractor unplugged after removing the rear bench
Restraint module coded for a three-seat third row on a two-seat vehicle
Squib of the centre retractor faulty
B00E8.d: B00E8 closes the C row of the table with the centre seat of the third row. No manufacturer publishes it, and the one public list that uses this block, Mercedes-Benz LI54.21-P-070658, stops at a left and a right third-row retractor (B00E7, B00E6). A centre tensioner in row three would mostly appear in large vans or SUVs with a three-seat rear bench. Joyson's retractor pretensioner is compact enough to go into a seat frame, which is where a centre unit would have to live. IIHS frontal tests of 2019 compared rear dummies in vehicles with standard belts and with tensioners plus load limiters, and noted such rear countermeasures are not yet widespread. If B00E8 is set, the airbag lamp is on and the centre belt is not tightened.
s: Airbag warning lamp illuminated
Centre seat of the third row without belt tensioning
Safety note: contains a pyrotechnic charge – no work without disconnecting the battery and waiting; leave it to a specialist workshop

c: Airbag module variant expects a driver inflatable belt that is not fitted
Plug of the belt gas generator at the lower anchor or seat loose or corroded
Lead to the inflator chafed by seat adjustment
Igniter of the belt inflator faulty
B00F0.d: B00F0 is the firing circuit for an inflatable belt at the driver's seat: a section of webbing that a gas source fills in a crash so the load spreads over a wider area of the chest. The production inflatable belts known from Ford and Mercedes-Benz sit only at rear outer seats; no carmaker documents B00F0. The idea for front seats is old and well described in patents, for example a Daimler design of 2010 with the gas generator at the lower anchor beside the B-pillar and folded webbing held by tear threads, and an Autoliv design with inflators mounted on the seat back. Joyson also lists a belt-attached restraint supplement among its airbag innovations. If the code is set, the airbag lamp comes on.
s: Airbag warning lamp on
Driver belt would not inflate in a crash
Safety note: the belt contains a pyrotechnic gas generator; work only de-energised (battery off, wait time) and at a specialist workshop

c: Module coded for a passenger inflatable belt that the car does not have
Connector at the buckle-side inflator under the passenger seat loose
Seat wiring damaged by objects under the seat or by seat movement
B00F1.d: B00F1 is the front passenger counterpart of B00F0, reserved for an inflatable belt at that seat. No manufacturer documents it, and no series vehicle is publicly known to have a passenger inflatable belt; Mercedes' S-Class manual offers the beltbag only for the outer rear belts. A passenger version would still face the same engineering choices as the patents show: Allied Chemical patented as early as 1972 a buckle that routes gas from a floor-mounted inflator through tongue and buckle into lap and shoulder belt, so the belt itself needs no wires, while Autoliv's 2002 design mounts separate inflators on the seat back. The airbag module would watch the igniter loop and set B00F1 for an open, a short or bad resistance.
s: Airbag lamp lit in the cluster
Passenger belt cannot inflate in a crash
Safety note: pyrotechnic belt inflator – disconnect the battery, respect the wait time and have repairs done by a specialist workshop

c: Internal wire damage in the second-row seat harness at the belt connector (Ford programme 21B11)
Plug of the inflator under the left rear seat loose after folding or removing the seat
Fault in the belt inflator igniter
B00F2.d: B00F2 covers the inflatable belt at the left outer seat of row two, the position where such belts actually reached production. Ford offered them from the 2011 Explorer; its 2018 owner's manual puts the bag into the shoulder part of the belts at both outer seats in row two, filled with cooled gas at lower pressure, deployed in frontal, side and rollover crashes and monitored by the same module and lamp as the front belts. Ford itself logs faults under its own codes B141B/B141C: programme 21B11 (Explorer 2014–2016) traces them to damaged seat harness wires at the rear inflatable belt connector. Mercedes-Benz fits its beltbag to the outer rear seats of the S-Class. Neither publishes B00F2. Airbag lamp on when set.
s: Airbag warning light on
Left rear inflatable belt may not deploy in a crash
Safety note: the belt holds a stored-gas or pyrotechnic inflator – battery off, wait time, work only at a specialist workshop

c: Restraint module configured for a centre inflatable belt not present in the vehicle
Connector at the centre buckle inflator under the bench disconnected
Igniter of the centre belt inflator open or shorted
B00F3.d: B00F3 refers to an inflatable belt at the centre seat of the second row. No manufacturer documents the code, and the known systems leave this seat out: Ford's 2018 Explorer manual limits its inflatable belts to the outermost second-row positions, and Mercedes fits its beltbag to the outer rear belts (S-Class manual 2017); the E-Class manual of the same year lists the belt air bag as a frontal-impact device. A centre version would be harder to package because the gas usually enters at the buckle or lower anchor; NHTSA's belt tensile study notes that the 2011 Explorer belt needed a retractor in the lap loop because its inflator was attached to the buckle. If set, the airbag lamp is lit.
s: Airbag indicator remains on
Rear centre belt would not inflate in a crash
Safety note: pyrotechnic or stored-gas inflator – only work with the battery disconnected and the wait time observed, at a specialist workshop

c: Worn or broken wires in the right second-row seat pigtail (Ford Explorer 2014–2016)
Inflator plug at the lower belt anchor or under the seat not latched
B00F4.d: B00F4 covers the inflatable belt on the outboard right seat of row two. The hardware exists in series cars, but the code is not documented by any maker. Ford's Explorer (2014–2016) logs belt faults as B141B and/or B141C; supplement 2 of programme 21B11 (June 2022) stresses checking those codes first and allows a separate labour time when both are present, then repositioning or replacing the seat harness pigtail. Mercedes-Benz offers the beltbag on rear belts of the E-Class; its manual warns against routing a child seat through a belt carrying the BELTBAG label. Daimler's 2010 patent places the gas generator at the lower belt anchor and folds the webbing with tear threads. With B00F4 set, the airbag lamp is on.
s: Airbag lamp illuminated
Right rear inflatable belt not ready to deploy
Safety note: do not open or probe the belt or its inflator; battery off, wait time, and leave the job to a specialist workshop

c: Airbag module coded with a third-row inflatable belt that is not installed
Plug at the left third-row belt inflator disturbed when folding the seat
Defective igniter in the third-row belt inflator
B00F5.d: B00F5 opens the third-row part of the inflatable-belt block with the left seat; B00F6 (centre) and B00F7 (right) follow. No manufacturer documents B00F5, and the known systems stop at row two: Ford's Explorer has its inflatable belts only at the second-row outer seats, even though it has a third row, and Mercedes offers the beltbag for rear belts of S- and E-Class (outer seats in the S-Class). The inflatable belt in NHTSA's 2021 test series was likewise a second-row belt. Technically a third-row unit would work like the others, with a bag in the shoulder webbing and an inflator near buckle or anchor, as the Autoliv patent outlines. If the code is stored, the airbag lamp is on and that belt will not inflate.
s: Airbag warning lamp on
Left third-row inflatable belt not available in a crash
Safety note: inflator with explosive igniter – disconnect the battery, wait, and have it handled by a specialist workshop

c: Airbag module coded for a centre third-row inflatable belt the vehicle does not have
Inflator plug of the centre belt loosened when the third-row seat was folded or removed
Igniter in the centre belt inflator out of its resistance window
B00F6.d: B00F6 names the deployment circuit for an inflatable belt at the middle seat of row three. That seat is the least likely place for such a belt: the series systems on record sit at outboard rear seats, Ford's Explorer only in row two and Mercedes' beltbag on the outer rear belts. The 2017 Mercedes GLS manual, for a three-row SUV, lists pyrotechnic tensioners and force limiters for its third-row belts, but no beltbag there. NHTSA's belt test series likewise used the inflatable Explorer belt from a second-row seat. Joyson's belt-attached restraint study for new interior layouts shows where such bags might spread. No maker publishes B00F6; if set, the airbag lamp is on and that belt would not inflate.
s: Airbag warning lamp lit
Centre third-row inflatable belt would not inflate in a crash
Safety note: igniter-equipped part – battery off, observe waiting time, work only in a specialist workshop

c: Chafed wires in the right rear seat harness, as seen one row forward on the Explorer (B141C)
Restraint module variant coding expects a right third-row inflatable belt
Open or shorted igniter in the right third-row belt inflator
B00F7.d: B00F7 closes the inflatable-belt block with the right seat of row three. No manufacturer documents it. The nearest real case is one row further forward: on the 2014–2016 Ford Explorer, the dealer bulletin for programme 21B11 names B141C as the right and B141B as the left second-row harness code and has technicians re-route or repair the seat pigtail when either appears. Ford's 2018 owner manual puts the rear inflatable belts in the shoulder webbing of the outboard second-row seats only; on the right of row three there are child-seat anchors but no bag. Mercedes lists beltbags for the outer rear belts of the S-Class, and Autoliv's 2002 patent shows one inflator feeding belts through a gas guide. With B00F7 present, the airbag lamp stays on.
s: Airbag lamp stays on after start-up check
Right third-row inflatable belt not armed
Safety note: never probe the inflator circuit with a test lamp; disconnect battery, wait, leave it to a specialist

c: Blower A motor worn, seized or with an open winding
Impeller blocked by ice, leaves or debris in the intake duct
Corroded or loose plug directly at blower A
B0100.d: B0100 is the general fault for air blower A in a sensor cleaning system, i.e. the fan or motor unit itself rather than its wiring or relay (those are B0102 and B0104). Such blowers keep camera lenses and lidar windows clear of droplets, dust and insects. Ford's patent US12115948B2 mounts a blower on the sensor bracket; it pulls outside air through an intake duct and pushes it out across a cylindrical lidar window and a camera lens. In Ford's roof-mounted sensor tiara for its self-driving test fleet, slots release an air curtain that deflects most bugs, and air also dries a lens after washing. Which blower is A is up to the maker. No vehicle manufacturer documents B0100 publicly. A dead blower lets dirt build up until the sensor reports itself blocked.
s: Sensor blocked or cleaning fault message
Driver assistance or automated driving functions limited or switched off
No airflow audible or felt at the sensor outlets

c: Blower or compressor B worn out or drawing too much current
Leaking or split air hose so blower B cannot build pressure
Water or salt ingress into blower B at an exposed mounting point
B0101.d: B0101 reports a fault of the second cleaning air source, blower B. A second unit makes sense where sensors are spread over the body: a roof pod and a bumper or corner sensor need separate air supplies. Not every design uses a fan; Uber's 2016 patent (now Aurora) feeds lidar and camera air knives from a compressor and accumulator held at about 140–160 psi, with one solenoid valve per outlet and a pressure sensor that raises a warning on a leak. AUMOVIO's lidar nozzles use compressed air to strip water droplets and to clear dust without washer fluid, and Kautex's Allegro systems combine water and air for camera and lidar. The split between A and B is not published by any carmaker, nor is B0101 itself.
s: Cleaning fault shown for the sensor group served by blower B
Water droplets or dust remain on lidar or camera window
Assistance functions reduced when the affected sensor goes blind

c: Broken control wire or pin between module and blower A
Control line of blower A shorted to ground or to battery voltage
Output stage in the cleaning or maintenance module defective
B0102.d: B0102 narrows the blower A problem down to its control path: the controlling module sees a wrong voltage or current on the line that commands blower A, typically an open circuit, a short to ground or a short to supply. In Ford's lidar cleaning patent US10569746B2 a computer opens airflow from a blower or compressor by driving an electric solenoid valve and may modulate it; when window opacity exceeds about 30 %, air runs first and autonomous mode may be dropped. Ford's later patent US12115948B2 places the blower beside the sensor on its bracket, so its feed runs into an exposed pod. Valeo notes that an obstructed lens can end automated operation.
